titleStmt.title: Timing-Anomaly Free Dynamic Scheduling of Periodic DAG Tasks with Non-Preemptive Nodes

analytic.title: Timing-Anomaly Free Dynamic Scheduling of Periodic DAG Tasks with Non-Preemptive Nodes

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Designing timing-anomaly free multiprocessor scheduling algorithms is a notoriously hard problem, especially for parallel tasks with non-preemptive execution regions. In this paper, we first propose a simple yet expressive model which abstracts a parallel task as a single computation unit, and then, present a sufficient condition for timing-anomaly free scheduling of such units. On top of this, we design an algorithm for scheduling a set of periodic parallel tasks, represented as DAG with non-preemptive subtasks, on multicore processors. The algorithm has several desirable properties, including timing-anomaly freedom, high resource utilization, and low memory requirement. Timing-anomaly freedom enables an exact schedulability test for the algorithm, which, as shown in our evaluations, provides a significantly high schedulability ratio compared to those state-of-the-art methods that suffer from timing anomalies.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: With the end of Moore's Law, the computer world has been rapidly developing in the direction of multi-core systems. Modern applications have to support parallel execution in order to exploit the computational resources provided by multicore systems thoroughly. Many parallel applications, such as OpenMP [11], and robotic software executed on ROS [10], can be naturally modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), in which nodes represent sequential execution units, also called subtasks, and edges represent precedence constraints between subtasks. Branches in a DAG characterize the parallelism in applications. Researchers have proposed various real-time scheduling algorithms and schedulability analysis methods for DAG-based task models.

We consider a recurring DAG task model, where DAG tasks regularly release DAG jobs, and nodes of a DAG execute nonpreemptively, but between the execution of any two nodes, the task can be preempted by other higher priority tasks. This preemption scheme is known as limited preemption [8], [35], meaning that a task can be preempted only at certain positions. Limited-preemptive scheduling can achieve a balanced tradeoff between fully preemptive (preemption can happen anywhere) and fully non-preemptive (no preemption is allowed) scheduling by avoiding expensive preemption overhead and long blocking delays due to lower priority tasks.

Two scheduling paradigms exist for scheduling the jobs of DAG tasks. Static scheduling [23], in which tasks are preassigned to fixed cores, fundamentally underutilizes resources due to load imbalance or communication overheads [36]. In contrast, dynamic scheduling can significantly improve resource utilization. However, dynamic scheduling suffers from timing anomalies [17], [26], [33], meaning that the worst-case response time of a DAG task can be longer if some subtasks' execution time is shorter than its worst-case execution time (WCET).

In this paper, we first generalize the conventional notion of non-preemptive jobs to parallel computation blocks (PCBs), which, as computation units, can occupy more than one core simultaneously. We derive a property under which a scheduling algorithm for PCBs is timing-anomaly free. Second, a dynamic scheduling algorithm, called DynFed, is proposed for limitedpreemptive recurring DAG tasks. The algorithm consists of two parts: (1) a precomputation phase, where the resource demand of each task, as well as an execution order among the nodes of each DAG task, is derived, and (2) a runtime phase, where tasks are scheduled using the precomputation data in a parallelized FIFO manner. The algorithm does not have to store a schedule of all the jobs released from DAG tasks, avoiding a high runtime memory requirement. Finally, by mapping DAG jobs onto PCBs, we prove that DynFed is timing-anomaly free. To the best of our knowledge, DynFed is the first timing-anomaly free dynamic (global) scheduling algorithm for the targeted model. It enables a simulation-based schedulability analysis where the exact worst-case response time of all recurring DAG tasks can be derived by simulating the jobs' execution according to their WCET. In our evaluations, the proposed algorithm exhibits significantly higher schedulability ratio compared to the state-of-the-art methods except for the table-driven approach.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. The related work is reviewed in Section I-A. The system model and a review on the timing anomaly are presented in Section II. Our model for abstracting the parallel workload of DAG tasks and a sufficient condition for timing-anomaly free scheduling for such a model are proposed in Section III. We propose the DynFed scheduling algorithm in Section IV, and prove its timing-anomaly freedom in Section V. Section VI evaluates the proposed approach in terms of schedulability compared with several of state-of-the-art methods. The paper concludes in Section VII by discussing potential extensions of the work.

div.head: A. Related Work
div.p: The schedulability analysis of non-preemptive sporadic tasks under global scheduling has been considered in several studies [4], [14], [18], [24]. However, these analysis methods are not designed for tasks with intra-task precedence constraints. One can apply them to such tasks by simplifying each task as a single non-preemptive component, which, however, can be highly pessimistic for many execution scenarios.

Real-time scheduling algorithms for DAG tasks have been studied in many works, which can be classified into three different paradigms: global scheduling [1], [6], [19], decomposition-based scheduling [20], [32], [34], and federated scheduling [2], [3], [25]. However, most of the existing works only consider fully preemptive or fully non-preemptive scheduling strategies.

Focusing on DAG tasks with limited preemption, Voudouris et al. [36] propose a timing-anomaly free scheduling algorithm for a single DAG by assigning each node in the DAG a fixed priority and then scheduling eligible nodes respecting their priority. This work has been generalized to tackle the scheduling of a single conditional DAG in [12]. This method can be applied to the federated scheduling [25] of multiple recurrent constrained-deadline DAGs by assigning each DAG a fixed number of dedicated cores on which its nodes are scheduled based on the proposed scheduler. However, it is unnecessarily pessimistic as all DAG are statically fixed on the dedicated cores and cannot run their jobs on other idle cores.

Several scheduling algorithms and schedulability analysis methods can be applied to the model we consider. A sufficient schedulability test targeting limited-preemptive sporadic DAG tasks scheduled by a global fixed-priority scheduler has been proposed by Serrano et al. [35]. It follows the standard response-time analysis scheme, which is fast but very pessimistic for periodic task sets as evaluated in [29]. Nasri et al. [29] present a schedulability analysis method based on state abstraction that explores all possible scheduling states with a merge strategy to accelerate. The experimental result shows that this method can distinguish most of the schedulable task sets. A potential limitation of this method is that it does not scale when the DAG tasks are highly parallel or the number of DAG tasks increases. In [9], Casini et al. propose a nodelevel partitioned fixed-priority scheduling algorithm and the corresponding schedulability analysis method. The proposed partitioned scheduling algorithm is timing-anomaly free, but the schedulability ratio drops to 0 on all the system settings after system utilization exceeds 50% due to the relatively lower resource utilization of partitioned scheduling compared with global scheduling when the task set has a high utilization.

div.head: II. PRELIMINARIES
div.p: This section presents the system model, notations, and a review of the concept of timing anomaly. In what follows, N and N + , respectively, denote the set of non-negative and positive integers.

div.head: A. System Model
div.p: We consider a set T = {τ 1 , • • • , τ n } of n periodic tasks executing on a system with m identical cores. Each task
div.formula: τ k is modeled by a DAG G k = (V k , E k ). V k = {v k,1 , . . . , v k,q k } is the set of nodes representing subtasks and E k ⊂ V k × V k is the set of edges among pairs of the subtasks representing precedence constraints. Node v k,j is a predecessor of v k,j if (v k,j , v k,j ) ∈ E k . Each node v k,j is associated with a WCET, denoted by c k,j ∈ N + . The total WCET of τ k is denoted by vol(τ k ) = q k j=1 c k,j . Each task τ k , assigned a deadline D k , releases an infinite sequence of jobs {J k,1 , J k,2 , • • • } with a period of T k ,
div.p: where the first job is released at time zero. A job, for instance J k,1 , comprises the subjobs {j k,1,1 , j k,2,1 , . . . , j k,q k ,1 } released from the subtasks of τ k . The execution of subjobs is non-preemptive, i.e., once a subjob starts to execute, it continues until completion. A subjob becomes ready for execution, called eligible, as soon as all its predecessors in the corresponding job are completed. For simplicity, we assume that the tasks have implicit deadlines, i.e., T k = D k , but our algorithm is also valid for the tasks with constrained deadlines. The hyperperiod of a task set is defined as the least common multiple (lcm) of the periods.

div.head: B. Timing Anomalies
div.p: Timing anomaly is a crucial problem in scheduling the described task model. Fig. 1 shows an example of a timing anomaly, in which two tasks τ 1 and τ 2 , with deadlines D 1 = 5 and D 2 = 10, are scheduled on two cores according to the global earliest deadline first (G-EDF) algorithm. The numbers upon the nodes represent the corresponding WCET. In Fig. 1(b), S 1 shows the schedule sequence for the first released jobs from τ 1 and τ 2 , when all subjobs run for their WCET (for brevity, the third index of the subjobs is omitted). Also, S 2 shows the schedule when the execution time of j 2,1 is 1. It is observed that the response time of τ 1 in S 2 is longer than that in S 1 , while the execution time of j 2,1 is shorter. Such a phenomenon is called timing anomaly and rules out analysis methods that rely on constructing the worst-case scenario since the real worst case is unknown in general.

We notice that timing anomaly essentially depends on the scheduling algorithm, e.g., G-EDF in Fig. 1. As it is too complicated to analyze the schedulers that involve timing anomaly efficiently, we instead consider the possibility of devising an efficient scheduling algorithm that can eliminate timing anomalies. Timing-anomaly free scheduling, analogous to the concept of sustainable scheduling in [7], is defined as follows.

Definition 1 (Timing-Anomaly Free Scheduling). A scheduler is timing-anomaly free if each task's response time under the WCET is always larger than or equal to its response time when some subjobs have execution times smaller than their WCET.
A simple way to avoid timing anomalies is to use the tabledriven scheduling in which an offline schedule is generated, and at runtime, exactly the same schedule is followed. If at

The response time of τ 1 in S 2 is larger than that in S 1 while the execution time of j 2,1 is shorter. runtime a subjob runs for shorter than its WCET, the respective core is left idle for the remaining time (until the expected WCET). This processor idling can be achieved by a set of timers. Using this approach faces a number of challenges. First, such timers (either software-based or hardware-based) may not be available to the scheduler. For instance, the on-board computer of the MIST research satellite does not provide timers [30]. Having software-level timers also requires a middleware layer that provides such facility, which is not necessarily the case in embedded real-time systems. Moreover, in the worst-case, we could have m timers programmed to idle all the m cores, which may not scale for large m, and handling the large number of timers' interrupts is not practical [36].

Another approach to achieve timing-anomaly free scheduling is based on the notion of execution order. In previous work, it is defined for a schedule of subjobs [12]. Here, we use a more general definition.

Definition 2 (Execution Order). Given a schedule of a group of computation units (e.g., subjobs, DAG jobs, etc.) I, an execution order O I is an order of all the units sorted with their starting times in a non-descending way.

As an example, consider the schedule S 1 in Fig. 1(b). An execution order for this schedule is O I = (j 1,1 j 2,1 j 1,2 j 1,3 j 2,2 ). Note that there exist multiple execution orders for a schedule of subjobs if some of the subjobs have the same starting time (as is the case in this example).

We say a scheduler follows an execution order O I if it dispatches the computation units (i.e., schedules them for execution) in the same order that they appear in O I . For a system with a single DAG task, it is shown in [12] that if the subjobs are always scheduled following the same execution order, regardless of the changes in execution times, the worstcase response time is obtained when all the subjobs run for their WCET. One can extend this result to the case of multitask systems, which is considered in the current work, by following the execution order of all subjobs in one hyperperiod. Although it would be a sound solution, this leads to an inevitable significant memory overhead when the hyperperiod is large. To avoid this, we relax the requirement of following a strict execution order among all subjobs. For this purpose, we first construct an abstract model to capture the resource requirement of parallel DAG tasks, as specified in Section III. Based on that, our timing-anomaly free scheduler is presented in Section IV.

div.head: III. A GENERIC MODEL FOR PARALLEL COMPUTATION
div.p: The timing anomaly described in Fig. 1 is caused by the fact that when, at time 2, j 1,3 becomes eligible, Core 2 is already occupied by the other task. This interference could be avoided if we had (temporarily) reserved the core for τ 1 . More generally, if upon the start of a task, we know the worst-case resource requirement of the task and reserve the cores based on that (until they are not needed anymore), then we can rule out anomalies that happen due to the variable interference of other tasks. In this section, we present a model to efficiently capture the resource requirement of a DAG task. We further present sufficient conditions for scheduling the respective abstract workloads in a timing-anomaly free manner. This is a general theoretical result, which also serves as a foundation for our timing-anomaly free scheduling algorithm in Section IV.

div.head: A. Parallel Computation Blocks
div.p: Conventionally, the elements that are scheduled, e.g., subjobs of a DAG, are computation units that need one processing core to run. We generalize this execution model by defining Parallel Computation Blocks as computational units that can occupy more than one core at a time. The resource demand of a PCB is non-preemptive, meaning that once a core is demanded, it will be dedicated to the PCB until it is not required anymore. Additionally, all cores that may be needed by the PCB are acquired upon its start; this is a crucial property to enable timing-anomaly free scheduling. Formally, the resource demand of a PCB is specified by a function as follows.

div.head: Definition 3 (Resource-Demand Function). The resourcedemand function (rdf) of a PCB is a function
div.p: is the number of cores demanded by the PCB t time units after it has started execution, satisfying the following property.

Example 1. Fig. 2(a) illustrates a possible schedule of τ 1 (specified in Fig. 1(a)) on two cores assuming no interfering workload. We can associate a PCB to this schedule if all required cores are demanded in the beginning. Fig. 2(b) shows the resulting rdf.

Worst-case rdf : Analogous to the notion of the WCET of ordinary real-time jobs, we define the worst-case rdf for a PCB as follows. Let R denote the set of possible rdf s that a PCB t rdf (t) may exhibit (due to execution variation and uncertainties). An rdf f is the worst-case rdf of the PCB if:

div.head: B. Timing-Anomaly Free Scheduling of PCBs
div.p: We target the scheduling of PCBs. Consider a PCB p with a worst-case rdf of f . In order for p to be scheduled and run, it must wait until at least f (0) number of cores are available. Once started, p acquires those cores. During the execution, at each instant t, the PCB demands a number of cores no more than f (t). Once a core is not required by the PCB anymore, it is released. Then, the scheduler can use the core to dispatch other PCBs. We restrict our attention to greedy scheduling of PCBs, defined below.

div.head: Definition 4 (Greedy scheduler). A scheduler is greedy if it continues to dispatch PCBs as long as the number of cores not demanded by any PCB is enough to dispatch the currently undispatched highest priority PCB.
div.p: As an example, Fig. 3 shows a greedy schedule of two PCBs p 1 and p 2 associated with jobs released by τ 1 and τ 2 in Fig. 1(a). (The precise connection between a DAG task and a PCB is discussed in the subsequent sections.)
We are interested in timing-anomaly free scheduling of PCBs. In the following, we show that this can be achieved by keeping a fixed execution order.

div.head: Lemma 1. Any greedy scheduler of PCBs that follows a fixed execution order is timing-anomaly free.
div.p: Proof. Assume a set of PCBs P, an associated execution order O P = p 1 . . . p |P| , and a greedy scheduler which dispatches the PCBs in the same order as O P . Let W denote the schedule produced when all PCBs have their worst-case rdf, and A be the schedule produced when one or several PCBs do not exhibit their worst-case rdf. The goal is to show that the completion time of each PCB in A is not later than that in W.

Let S w i and S i denote the start time of the PCB p i ∈ P in W and A, respectively. Due to the non-preemptive execution of PCBs, it suffices to show S i ≤ S w i for 1 ≤ i ≤ |P|. We show this by induction on i.

Base case (i = 1): In the beginning, no PCB is running. Thus, p 1 is always dispatched instantly, i.e., S 1 = S w 1 = 0, which implies S 1 ≤ S w 1 . Induction step: Assume the result holds for some i ≥ 1, that is, S j ≤ S w j for all j, 1 ≤ j ≤ i. We show S i+1 ≤ S w i+1 . If, in A, p i+1 is dispatched before S w i+1 , the property holds trivially. Therefore, we consider the situation where, in A, p i+1 is not dispatched before S w i+1 . Let f k denote the rdf of p k ∈ P. The total number of cores occupied by PCBs at S w i+1 just before
div.formula: p i+1 is dispatched is computed, in W, by 1≤k≤i f k (S w i+1 -S w k ), and in A by 1≤k≤i f k (S w i+1 -S k ). By induction hypothesis, we know S k ≤ S w k , for 1 ≤ k ≤ i, which means S w i+1 -S k ≥ S w i+1 -S w k . This, in conjunction with the rdf 's property in (1), implies f k (S w i+1 -S k ) ≤ f k (S w i+1 -S w k ), and hence, 1≤k≤i f k (S w i+1 -S k ) ≤ 1≤k≤i f k (S w i+1 -S w k ).(3)
div.p: This means that the number of cores occupied in A (the lefthand side of (3)) is not larger than that in W. As a result, in A the PCB p i+1 is dispatched at S w i+1 (as the scheduler is greedy), which completes the proof. Lemma 1 establishes an important advantage of using the PCB abstraction: the variations in the execution time of a task can be kept local, avoiding undesired anomalous interference on other tasks, as long as the following two conditions hold:

1) the resource usage of each PCB (or equivalently, the corresponding task) does not exceed its worst-case rdf, 2) the PCBs are scheduled in a greedy and "execution-order preserving" way. In the next section, we present a scheduling algorithm in which each DAG job's demand can be modeled by an rdf, and thus, each job is a PCB. As it is shown in Section V, the algorithm preserves the execution order, which reveals it as a timing-anomaly free scheduler for periodic DAG tasks.

div.head: IV. DYNAMIC-FEDERATED SCHEDULING
div.p: The main idea of the dynamic-federated (DynFed) scheduler is to statically analyze each task to find a bound on its resource demand. The scheduler then guarantees that at runtime the required resource will be received by the tasks. The algorithm consists of two parts: (1) a precomputation phase, where the resource demand that each task requires to meet deadlines is derived, and (2) a runtime phase, where tasks are scheduled using the precomputation data in a timinganomaly free manner.

div.head: A. Precomputation
div.p: Precomputation is an offline phase where we try to schedule each task individually with a minimum number of cores, assuming that the nodes run for their WCET. This can be done by any scheduling algorithm which efficiently, in terms of the number of cores, schedules a single DAG. The precomputation procedure is shown in Alg. 1 which computes three items for any given task τ k . First, the minimum number of cores required to schedule τ k , denoted by m min k , is computed through Lines 1 to 4. As seen, m min k is initialized (in Line 1) by a minimum possible number of cores required to meet the deadline in an idealistic case where all the workload can be executed fully in parallel. If the computed number of cores is not adequate for the task to meet the deadline using the considered scheduler, m min k is iteratively incremented until the task is schedulable. In order to examine if the computed number of cores is adequate, Line ) can be computed by simulating the execution of a single instance of the task where all nodes run for their WCET. We can rely on the response time computed in this way due to the timing-anomaly freedom of the scheduler, shown in Section V.

In Line 5, the schedule obtained from applying the scheduler to τ k with m min k cores is computed. The schedule is used in Line 6 to compute a set V end k , whose elements are used at runtime as an indication to when a core is not needed by the task anymore (see the next subsection for the details). The corresponding execution order is also stored in O k .

Note that from line 1 to 4, the algorithm is minimizing the number of cores a task needs based on its deadline by allocating the corresponding subjobs into as few cores as possible. This potentially reduces the resource waste for DAG tasks having a "parallel burst" structure, e.g., a DAG starting from a source node with a large WCET followed by many parallel successor nodes. The reason lies in the mechanism of DynFed presented in the next subsection. ) is invoked to compute the response time assuming nodes' WCET. The resulting schedule is seen in Fig. 2(a), which gives RT (τ k , m min k ) = 5 ≯ D 1 , and hence, the while loop is skipped. Then, according to the obtained schedule, i.e., the one in Fig. 2(a), Line 6 computes
div.formula: m min k ← m min k + 1 4: end while 5: S ← schedule(τ k , m min k ) 6: V end k ← {v k,j ∈ V k | once v k,j finished, the corresponding core is never used in S thereafter } 7: O k ← V k sorted
div.p: The data that is computed in precomputation needs to be stored and used at runtime. For a task τ k , this includes m min k , which is a single integer value, in addition to an execution order and the set V end k ⊆ V k , both of which entail a memory overhead which linearly grows with the number of task's nodes. The next section shows how this data is used in the online scheduling.

div.head: B. Job Dispatching
div.p: At runtime, the algorithm schedules DAG jobs according to a first-in first-out (FIFO) policy. Jobs are allowed to be computed in parallel but in a controlled way: once a job is started, its resource utilization is confined, based on the precomputed data, so as to prevent anomalous interference on other jobs.

The procedure is specified in Alg. 2, which is invoked whenever a new DAG job is released, or a running subjob completes. We assume that whenever a new DAG job, denoted by J k,i , is released, and before the algorithm is invoked, the job is placed in a FIFO queue, and it is set started (J k,i ) = False. The FIFO queue breaks the ties between the jobs with the same arrival time in a deterministic way (e.g., by a fixed priority assigned to the tasks). In Alg. 2, m k is used to keep the number of cores that currently run a subjob of τ k , and m ded k to denote the number of cores currently dedicated to the task (but not necessarily running a subjob of τ k at the moment). Note that it always holds: m k ≤ m ded k . The algorithm consists of three parts. First, through Lines 2 to 5, the subjobs that have just finished are treated. This consists of decrementing the respective m k , and also decrementing m ded k if the finished node is a member of V end k . Decreasing m ded k by one indicates that the core that has been running the subjob will not be needed by the respective job anymore, and it can be safely used to run subjobs of other tasks.

Second, through the while loop, and in a FIFO manner, the DAG jobs for which there is enough resource will be selected to start. In Line 9, m -n k=1 m ded k denotes the number of idle cores, i.e., those not dedicated to any task, and thus,
div.formula: m min k > m - n k=1 m ded k
div.p: means that the number of available cores is not enough to start τ k at the moment. As a result, the procedure does not continue subjob dispatching and quits the loop. On the other hand, if there are enough cores to start the job, it is removed from the queue and is flagged as started (Lines 12 and 13), which is an indication for the next part, explained shortly. Also, the value m min k is assigned to m ded k , meaning that m min k cores are temporarily reserved for the job. In the third part of the algorithm, i.e., Lines 17 to 31, the subjobs of each task are dispatched, respecting the order O k , as long as the resource limit for the task is not exceeded. This is validated by examining m k < m ded k (Line 23). As seen, DynFed schedules the jobs in two levels. The joblevel scheduling, corresponded with Lines 7 to 15 in Alg. 2, is based on FIFO with a deterministic tie breaking, which implies a fixed order among the jobs. The subjob-level scheduling, expressed in Lines 17 to 31, is also based on the order derived in precomputation. Based on the two level scheduling, the next section shows that DynFed is timing-anomaly free.

div.head: V. ANOMALY FREEDOM OF DY NFE D
div.p: The goal is to show that, given any task set, under DynFed scheduling, the worst-case completion time of the jobs happens when all subjobs run for their WCET. We refer to the schedule obtained in this scenario by W, and the schedule obtained when some subjobs run shorter than WCET as A. The proof contains two parts. We first focus on the finish time of subjobs with respect to the start time of the corresponding job.

div.head: Definition 5 (Relative finish time). The relative finish time of a subjob is its finish time relative to the time the first subjob of the same job is dispatched.
div.p: We show that the relative finish time of a subjob in A is not larger than that in W.

div.head: Lemma 2. Under DynFed, the relative finish time of each subjob is worst case in W.
div.p: Proof. Consider an arbitrary job consisting of subjobs j 1 , . . . , j q k , where subjobs are indexed according to their execution order in DynFed. Let S w i and S i denote the start time of the i-th subjob relative to the job's start time, in W and A, respectively. Due to non-preemptive execution of subjobs, it suffices to show that S i ≤ S w i , for 1 ≤ i ≤ q k . We prove this by induction on i.

The relation holds for i = 1 because the first subjob always starts with a zero offset compared to the job start time, that is, S 1 = S w 1 = 0, as there is no interfering subjob. Let the property hold for subjobs j 1 to j i . We then prove S i+1 ≤ S w i+1 by contradiction. For this, assume S i+1 > S w i+1 . Let V w (S w i+1 ) be the set of subjobs running at S w i+1 in W just before j i+1 is dispatched. Also, let V (S w i+1 ) denote the set of subjobs running at S w i+1 in A after all subjobs j 1 to j i have been dispatched (they are all dispatched due to the induction hypothesis). Then, we have V (S w i+1 ) ⊆ V w (S w i+1 ). The reason is that V (S w i+1 ) may contain only subjobs j 1 , . . . , j i (due to in-order execution of subjobs, and since j i+1 is not yet dispatched); and from these subjobs, all who are done by S w i+1 in W are so in A due to the induction hypothesis. In other words, all not in V w (S w i+1 ) are also not in V (S w i+1 ), which means V (S w i+1 ) ⊆ V w (S w i+1 ). Next, it is shown that under DynFed scheduling and using Lemma 2, each DAG follows the notion of a PCB. Lemma 3. Under DynFed , each DAG job can be viewed as a PCB which exhibits its worst-case rdf when all subjobs get their WCET.

Proof. We need to show that the resource demand of the jobs follows conditions (1) and ( 2). The first condition asks for a non-increasing resource demand. As the resource demand (i.e., number of cores) of a task τ k is kept by m ded k (Alg. 2), the first condition holds by observing that after m ded k is initialized (in Line 14), it is only decremented (Line 4). This means that the resource demand (which can be abstracted by an rdf ) is worst case (greatest) in W.

Proof. According to Lemma 3, under DynFed, each subjob follows the properties of a PCB. As a result of this and the fact that DynFed is greedy, Lemma 1 applies, which implies that in DynFed all jobs experience their worst-case finish time in the schedule W. This, together with Lemma 2, implies that all subjobs experience their worst-case finish time in W, which completes the proof.
Theorem 1 enables an exact schedulability test for DynFed as discussed below.

div.head: A. Schedulability Test
div.p: According to Theorem 1, the worst-case response time of the tasks is obtained when all the subjobs execute for their WCET. Hence, the worst-case response time of the tasks can be computed by simulating the system execution under DynFed for one hyperperiod. Comparing the obtained response time of each task with its deadline determines whether the task is schedulable or not. This analysis is tight because there exists an actual scenario which leads to the computed response times.

The complexity of simulating the system for one hyperperiod can be exponential. However, industrial applications, such as the one reported in [22], are usually subject to periods that lead to an affordable hyperperiod.

div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: We evaluate DynFed in terms of its ability to successfully schedule task sets. 1 For this, we apply the method to a set of randomly generated task sets, and measure the acceptance ratio, which is defined as the number of task sets deemed to be schedulable divided by the total number of task sets.

For the DAG structures, we consider series-parallel (SP) graphs [31], which are used by other studies [9], [29], [35] as a flexible and expressive model. To generate random SP graphs, we employ the algorithm proposed in [31]. This involves a recursive procedure that starts with a pair of source and sink 1 The evaluation source code is publicaly available at https://github.com/mortezamohaqeqi/dynfed. nodes. At each invocation, the input pair are connected either by simply inserting an intermediate node (with probability p term ), or a parallel branch (with probability 1p term ). In the latter case, the two ending points of each branch are recursively fed to the procedure. The number of branches in this case is randomly chosen from [2, n par ]. After the primary structure is created, an edge is also added between any pair of nodes with probability p add (if it does not lead to a cycle). The WCET of each node is randomly chosen from [1,50].

For period assignment, we follow the same approach used in [29]. Based on this, to each task τ k a utilization u k is assigned according to the UUnifast algorithm [5], and then, the closest number to vol (τ k )/u k from a set T (defined shortly) is selected as the period. Then, the WCETs of τ k are scaled to make the utilization equal to u k . Since WCETs are supposed to be integers, when scaling, the obtained values are rounded to the closest non-zero integer. In this method, periods are chosen from the set [29]

The motivation is that T contains periods with three different orders of magnitude, which is essential for a fair comparison of scheduling algorithms [13]. Also, it covers periods that are found in automotive applications [22].

To evaluate different methods, we vary the utilization from 20% to 100% with the steps of 5%. For each utilization point, 1250 random task sets have been evaluated. As the single-task scheduler in the precomputation phase of DynFed (Alg. 1), we employed a least-laxity approach [28] with these steps:

1) Pick the eligible node that has least laxity, 2) Schedule the node to start at the earliest possible time, 3) Go to step 1 if there is still an unscheduled node. The laxity of a node v k,j is defined as T kcp k,j where cp k,j is recursively defined as:
div.formula: cp k,j = c k,j , v k,j is sink, c k,j + max{cp k,l |v k,l ∈ Succ(v k,j )}, otherwise
div.p: in which Succ(v k,j ) denotes the set of nodes to which there is an edge from v k,j . A node v k,j is sink if Succ(v k,j ) is empty.
We compare DynFed with the following methods:

• Federated Lazy: The federated scheduling algorithm proposed in [36] where to each task, a minimum number of required cores is dedicated. In this method, the Lazy scheduling algorithm [36] is used to compute the minimum number of cores needed to successfully schedule a task when executed individually. • RM: The analytical method for schedulability analysis of global fixed-priority scheduling proposed in [35], where we assign higher priorities to tasks with shorter periods. • EDF: The analytical method proposed in [29], where jobs are prioritized according to the G-EDF policy. In addition to WCETs of the nodes, that method uses the best-case execution times (BCET) of the nodes as an input parameter. As the other methods that are used for comparison do not make any assumption with respect to the values of BCET, we set the BCET of all the nodes to be 0 when using this method.

• Table-Driven: A scheduler that executes the nodes according to their WCETs. If the execution time of a node is less than its WCET, the running core is left idle until the time at which the node was supposed to finish based on its WCET. In this approach, eligible nodes are prioritized by the absolute deadline of the job they belong to. Nodes with the same deadline are prioritized by their laxity. • DynFed (BFS): Another version of DynFed where for the single-task scheduler, a breadth-first search (BFS) order is used to prioritize the nodes instead of their laxity. A BFS order is a list of the nodes in which all predecessors of a node come before the node itself. Ties are broken randomly; however, after ties are broken, a unique list is obtained which defines a fixed and unique priority for each node. • FP-FIFO: A FIFO scheduling where a new DAG job may start only when the previous ones are completed. Ties are broken by giving higher priority to smaller periods. Nodes of a DAG are scheduled in a fixed order obtained from a laxity-based scheduling specified above. FP-FIFO is also timing-anomaly free because the execution order of all the subjobs is preserved.

It is important to note that the competitive methods Federated Lazy, RM, and EDF are not exactly for the same settings that we consider in this paper. More precisely, Federated Lazy [36] and RM [35] have been proposed for a more general task model, i.e., sporadic tasks; EDF [29] exploits the information about BCET, while here we disabled this capability. However, as these methods consider the closest model to ours, we use them for comparison.

As the simulation platform, we have used a system with 32 GiB of RAM and 20 logical computing cores. In the following, we first present the results for a rather general task set parameters in Section VI-A where we exclude the EDF method. The reason is that this method uses a state-space exploration approach demanding for a very large scale memory (multiple clusters each with 256 GiB RAM as reported in [29]) and it did not reveal a result on our simulation platform even for one task set. As a result, we provide the corresponding results for a configuration with smaller tasks in Section VI-B.

div.head: A. The General Case
div.p: In this section, we use mainly the same parameter settings used in [29], i.e., p term = 0.4, p add = 0.1, the maximum number of nested branches = 3 (i.e., the maximum number of nodes in a path of DAG will be 7). Further, we set n par = 6.

The results are seen in Fig. 4. First, we note that among the evaluated methods, RM and Federated Lazy consider sporadic tasks. As a result, it is reasonable that they exhibit smaller acceptance ratio compared to a method which exploits the fact that the tasks are periodic. As seen in Fig. 4, RM performs poorly in terms of acceptance ratio. This is partially rooted in the mentioned remark. In addition, the restriction of the period values to the set T defined in (6), where many values are a multiple of the others, worsens the situation in terms of acceptance ratio.

It is seen that FP-FIFO also has a very low acceptance ratio, mainly because it does not exploit the inter-task parallelism. Meanwhile, the method performs slightly better when the number of tasks is small, i.e., n = 10. The reason lies in the fact that this method can properly exploit the intra-task parallelism, and in the mentioned case, individual task scheduling plays a more important role in the overall performance.

The Federated Lazy method exhibits promising results in most cases. Basically, this method dedicates at least one core to each task. As a result, it is expected to observe an acceptance ratio of zero whenever there are more tasks than the cores. This is not seen in our results, however, since to improve the performance, before applying the method, we have always combined the tasks with the same period into a single task. The main practical advantage of this method is that the tasks are executed on dedicated cores avoiding undesirable interference. Meanwhile, this is also its major disadvantage which may waste the resource for small tasks. This happens particularly in the settings of Fig. 4(d), i.e., when the number of tasks relative to the cores is the largest.

It is seen that with an increased number of cores (from 8 to 32), the relative performance of DynFed improves. It can be attributed to the fact that with a higher number of cores, DynFed finds more cores available, helping it eliminate the undesired effect of non-preemptive executions which cause a higher priority task to be blocked by lower priority ones.
Finally, Table-Driven always achieves a high number of schedulable task sets. This can be considered as a kind of ideal case by which other methods can be compared.

div.head: B. Small Task Sets
div.p: To keep the size of the problem state space amenable for the EDF method, in this section we use the following parameters: p term = 0.7, p add = 0.1, the maximum number of nested branches = 2 (i.e., the maximum number of nodes in a path will be 5), and n par = 3. The performance of different schedulability analysis methods is seen in Fig. 5.

According to the results, the method EDF outperforms the other analytical approach, i.e., RM, which can be related to the extensive exploration of possible scheduling scenarios. In comparison, DynFed shows a substantially higher acceptance ratio gained from the timing-anomaly freedom of the algorithm, which enables a simulation-based schedulability analysis. In other words, when DynFed is used, we exactly know the worst-case scenario, by which we can efficiently avoid the pessimism that exists in other analysis methods.

Fig. 5(b) shows an exception in the performance of Table-Driven. As seen, there are situations where DynFed can successfully schedule a task set while Table-Driven fails. Fig. 5(b) presents the results of a configuration where the number of tasks, and thus, the number of subjobs to be scheduled, is low. This means that the units that are to be scheduled (i.e., the non-preemptive subjobs) are relatively coarse grained. This makes it more difficult for the schedulers to schedule the tasks (one can think of such scheduling as a bin-packing problem with large items). As a result, it is more likely that global schedulers, such as Table-Driven, fail to successfully schedule a task set. In comparison, approaches such as DynFed and Federated Lazy forecast the required resources and can avoid deadline miss in some cases.

div.head: VII. CONCLUDING REMARKS
div.p: The paper addresses the problem of scheduling a set of recurring DAG tasks with non-preemptive nodes upon a multicore platform. Based on an abstraction of the resource demand of the computation units, we present a timing-anomaly free dynamic scheduling algorithm for the model. Benefiting from the precomputation, DynFed demands a relatively lower online memory requirement compared with static methods that have to store the running order of all the subjob instances in a hyperperiod, and lower runtime overhead as the jobs are running non-preemptively. The evaluation shows that the proposed algorithm exhibits significantly higher schedulability ratio compared to the state-of-the-art methods except for the table-driven approach.

Although our method can waste resources because of reservation, this resource loss is lower compared to the partitioning or federated scheduling approaches which statically dedicate the cores to the tasks. In fact, DynFed improves the resource utilization by allowing dynamic reservation and release of the cores. At the same time, it provides higher timing predictability compared to the fully dynamic schedulers, such as G-EDF, thanks to the resource reservation and also preserving the execution order of subjobs.

The proposed approach can be extended to a more general case where the tasks are subject to release jitters. In such situation, DynFed still works as long as the release jitter does not change the execution order of the PCBs, or, we let the scheduler consciously wait for a delayed higher priority job before dispatching lower priority jobs.

For future work, two potential directions can be considered. First, when the BCET of the nodes are known a priori, the resource utilization of DynFed can be improved by utilizing the reserved but idle cores to other jobs if the timing-anomaly freedom is not broken. This can potentially remedy the waste of resources of long reservation. Second, in DynFed, PCBs are prioritized based on their release times, limiting the schedulability when dispatching a job with a larger absolute deadline ahead of other jobs. How to break the order and still enjoy timing-anomaly freedom is an interesting problem.
